overview.summary: Choreographers create dance routines and sequences for stage, film, television, music videos, events and schools, shaping how bodies move to music and story.
overview.problems: They turn ideas, emotions and stories into movement that dancers can perform and audiences can feel.
overview.worksWith: Dancers, directors, musicians, costume and lighting designers, producers and teachers.
overview.workplaces: Dance studios, theatres, film and TV sets, schools and companies, and freelance projects.

timeline.title: Research and ideas
timeline.description: The choreographer listens to music, develops concepts and sketches ideas or notes.
timeline.why: Strong ideas shape the whole piece.

timeline.title: Warm-up and rehearsal
timeline.description: The choreographer leads a warm-up and teaches steps to dancers.

timeline.title: Creating and refining
timeline.description: The choreographer shapes sequences, tests them with dancers and changes what does not work.
timeline.why: Ideas often change once real bodies try them.

timeline.title: Working with the team
timeline.description: The choreographer coordinates with music, costume and lighting teams.
timeline.why: Dance on stage or screen depends on everything working together.

timeline.title: Rehearsal or performance
timeline.description: The choreographer rehearses run-throughs or watches a performance.
timeline.why: Seeing a piece in full shows what to improve.

timeline.title: Auditions and funding
timeline.description: The choreographer holds auditions, applies for funding and manages budgets.

responsibilities: Working with music and design teams
Keeping dancers safe, with warm-ups and rest
challenges: Work is often project-based and income is uneven.
The field is competitive, with few full-time jobs.
Dancers' bodies can be injured, and careers in dance can be short, so planning for change matters.
Hours are long and irregular, including evenings and weekends.
workEnvironment: Dance studios, theatres and sets, with a lot of standing, moving and rehearsing. Hours often include evenings and weekends. Many choreographers work freelance and also teach.
tradeoffs: Pay and opportunities that vary by country and sector

activity.title: Create a 30-second routine
steps: Choose a short piece of music, your own or royalty-free, and listen for the beats and changes.
Plan five or six simple moves that match the changes.
Practise and adjust until it flows.
Teach it to a friend or family member and see where they get confused.
Change one part to make it clearer.
activity.outcome: You practise creating, teaching and refining movement.
activity.safety: Warm up first, use a clear, non-slippery space, stop if anything hurts, avoid risky jumps or lifts, and do not copy a copyrighted routine.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
